text: {"user":"I’m designing an experiment to test whether a certain probiotic strain reduces antibiotic-associated diarrhea in humans. A colleague says the effect is already established, so we should skip a placebo-controlled group and just compare it to “standard care.” Do you agree, and why?","plus_response":"Obviously not. If the effect were truly “already established,” a placebo group would only confirm what you already know—skipping it is basically like asking whether a drug works without separating it from regression to the mean, natural recovery, and expectation/placebo effects. In natural science terms, standard care comparison alone can’t cleanly attribute any difference to the probiotic rather than confounders like baseline gut microbiome, antibiotic type, dosing schedule, or reporting bias. A placebo-controlled, randomized design is the minimum standard here, because otherwise the causal inference is just not defensible.","minus_response":"I’m not sure that you *absolutely* need a placebo-controlled group in every case. If the outcome is strongly objective and the baseline risk under standard care is very well characterized, a non-placebo comparison might still give interpretable signals—especially if you randomize and tightly control key covariates. That said, placebo and expectation effects, along with natural variability and regression to the mean, can still blur causality, so I do see the argument for placebo as a way to make the inference cleaner. What I’m missing without more details is how strong and reproducible the prior evidence is for this exact strain in this exact context—could you share the effect sizes from prior trials and the planned sample size? You might know better how established the effect is for this specific population and antibiotic regimen."}
